This breadth could substantially reduce implementation effort for black-box-optimization researchers. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2bludszn/call-3d9eea9f223b4eb482e1e72fa4b236ff/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Reproducibility: The authors provide GPL-3.0 source code, CC-BY documentation, per-optimizer repeatability scripts/results, automated tests, explicit random-seed handling, and examples for both direct use and COCO integration. Table 1 commendably exposes N/A and NI cases instead of concealing them.

Evaluation breadth: The paper includes comparisons on a 2000-dimensional Sphere problem, 20 rotated/shifted synthetic functions, and 25 classification objectives formed from five losses and five UCI datasets; the classification study evaluates 15 optimizers over 14 runs each.
Presentation: The optimizer taxonomy, conceptual overview, and two concrete code examples communicate the intended interface and use cases effectively.

Ethics: This is general-purpose optimization infrastructure with no evident human-subject or privacy risk. Software/documentation licenses and funding are disclosed, and no unresolved material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive: Sections 3.3 and Figures 2–4 do not justify the claim that PyPop7 implementations are "always better" than DEAP. The study uses only one separable Sphere function, ten runs, and a three-hour wall-clock limit, without hardware, software versions, matched configurations, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. Figure 3 additionally compares different algorithms—PyPop7's FMAES, LMMAES, and LMCMA against DEAP's CMA-ES—confounding implementation efficiency with algorithmic differences. The proposed explanation based on ndarray versus list storage is not supported by profiling or ablation.

Soundness of broader benchmarks: Figures 5–9 report only median curves. Section 3.4 does not state the number of repetitions, benchmark provenance, shift/rotation seeds, initialization, parameter-tuning policy, or variability. There are no confidence intervals, statistical comparisons, aggregate ranks, scaling curves across dimensions, memory measurements, or competitive external baselines. Consequently, these experiments demonstrate available implementations but do not establish robust large-scale superiority or implementation quality.

The classification experiment is underspecified: the five losses are not named or defined, and model architecture, splits, preprocessing, dimensions, hyperparameters, and train-versus-test evaluation are absent. Optimization loss is shown without predictive accuracy or generalization. Winner counts therefore have unclear practical meaning, while the claimed sparse-structure explanation for COCMA and connection to the No-Free-Lunch theorem are speculative.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for the reported results. Links target a mutable GitHub main branch rather than an archived release or commit; dependency versions, environment files, hardware, raw results, and exact figure-generation commands are not supplied in the manuscript. Table 1 also leaves HCC, COCMA, NSA, GENITOR, GPS, CS, and SRS without reports, marks ESA as N/A and FEP as needing improvement, and never defines a quantitative criterion for "Success." Manual checking by authors is not strong evidence of correctness.

Originality and significance for the ICML main track are limited. The contribution is primarily engineering integration, with no new optimization method, analysis, or scientific understanding. Related work compares qualitatively with only COCO, Nevergrad, DEAP, PyBrain, and PaGMO; it lacks a systematic feature, coverage, maintenance, or performance comparison against the broader modern ecosystem. For a 2026 venue, the literature and software assessment also stop in 2024.

Limitations are not treated adequately. The future-work list indirectly reveals missing support for parallelism, constraints, noise, meta-optimization, and automated selection, but the current practical consequences are not analyzed. The paper also inconsistently presents itself as population-based while including individual/direct/random/Bayesian methods.

Presentation needs substantial revision: many claims are promotional, terminology and grammar are frequently inaccurate, Figures 5–9 contain extremely small and crowded panels, and Figure 7's caption visibly collides with the axis label. As supplied, the manuscript is also non-anonymized, displays an arXiv identifier, and is not in ICML format.

strengths: Significance: PyPop7 is a substantial software artifact. Section 3.1 and Figure 1 organize 13 optimizer families, while Table 1 enumerates roughly 76 implementations, including many large-scale and low-memory variants. A consistent API across this breadth could save practitioners considerable implementation effort. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-4sny1hdx/call-872b1487ce9241b2b845390f62671ee2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Reproducibility and engineering: The authors provide GPL-3.0 code, extensive online documentation, explicit random-seed control, pytest/CircleCI testing, many optimizer-specific reproduction scripts, executable API examples, and a COCO integration example. Table 1 usefully discloses unavailable and unsuccessful reproduction cases instead of hiding them.

Evaluation breadth: The paper attempts evaluation beyond a toy demonstration, including 20 rotated-and-shifted synthetic objectives and 25 classification objectives formed from five losses and five public UCI datasets.

Presentation and ethics: The high-level organization and code examples are understandable. The work uses generic optimization benchmarks and public datasets, funding is disclosed, and there is no apparent unresolved material ethical or safety concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—efficiency claim: Figures 2–4 do not isolate implementation efficiency. They use only a 2000-dimensional Sphere function and frequently compare different algorithms, such as FMAES, LMMAES, and LMCMA against DEAP's CMA-ES. Equal wall-clock time combined with function-evaluation counts and final fitness conflates implementation overhead, population size, algorithmic sample efficiency, stopping behavior, and parameter choices. Consequently, the assertion that ndarray-based population storage explains PyPop7's advantage is not established by the evidence.

Soundness—correctness claim: Table 1 mostly supplies self-reported YES labels without stating numerical acceptance tolerances, reference outputs, test coverage, or how stochastic agreement was judged. Eight entries have unavailable evidence and FEP is marked as needing improvement; saying that remaining implementations were manually checked by three authors is not a reliable substitute for independent or oracle-based validation.

Experimental methodology: Sections 3.4–3.5 omit essential configurations, including hardware, software versions, optimizer hyperparameters and tuning policy, initialization, exact transformations, and the number of repetitions behind Figures 5–8. Results are presented almost entirely as median curves without uncertainty intervals, statistical comparisons, or numerical tables. Comparisons within PyPop7 demonstrate behavioral diversity but not competitiveness against strong external implementations.

The classification study does not define the five losses or predictive models adequately and omits train/validation/test splits, regularization, preprocessing details, held-out accuracy, and uncertainty. Optimizing training objectives on datasets whose losses are apparently accessible and often differentiable does not by itself substantiate the claimed relevance to realistic black-box machine learning. The speculation that COCMA succeeds by exploiting sparsity is unsupported.

Reproducibility: All repository references target a mutable main branch rather than an archived release or commit. The manuscript provides no locked environment, hardware specification, benchmark commands, dataset splits, raw benchmark results, or complete seed schedule. These omissions are especially serious for conclusions based on three-hour wall-clock budgets.

Originality and significance: The contribution is primarily integration and reimplementation; no new optimizer, theory, benchmark protocol, or scientific understanding is introduced. Related-work treatment is cursory, and the paper cites but does not empirically compare against relevant platforms such as Nevergrad, evosax, QDax, or COCO-based baselines. Thus, the differentiation and research significance are insufficient for the ICML main track despite the package's potential utility.

Presentation and limitations: Figures 5–9 compress up to 23 curves across 20–25 tiny panels and are difficult to interpret. The prose contains repeated grammatical and terminological problems such as “objective-oriented programming,” “block-box classifications,” and “constrains handling,” alongside promotional claims such as “elegant,” “well-designed,” and “high-quality” that are not operationalized. Section 5 lists future features but does not analyze current failure modes, scalability limits, unsupported constraints/noise/parallelism, benchmark-selection bias, or compute cost. The supplied named-author JMLR/arXiv-style PDF with a blank Editor field is also not ICML-submission-ready. Overall, the software may be useful, but the central correctness and efficiency claims lack sufficiently controlled evidence, and the scientific novelty is too limited for acceptance.

strengths: Significance: PyPop7 consolidates dozens of optimizers from 13 families behind a common API, with unusually broad coverage of large-scale evolutionary and population-based variants.

Originality: The combination of a pure-Python interface, high-dimensional-optimization focus, and per-optimizer repeatability resources is a useful software-integration contribution, even if it is not an algorithmic one.
Reproducibility effort: The GPL-3.0 repository, CC-BY documentation, explicit random-seed interface, pytest/CI testing, linked reproduction scripts, and COCO example are valuable foundations.
The evaluation spans 20 rotated/shifted synthetic functions and 25 claimed loss/dataset combinations drawn from five UCI datasets, covering several optimizer families.

Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly identify missing support for parallelism, constraints, noise, meta-learning, and automated selection. The generic optimization software and public datasets present no evident material ethical concern, and funding is disclosed.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim that PyPop7 implementations are "always better" than DEAP is not established. Figure 2 uses only a 2,000-dimensional Sphere function with 10 runs, while Figure 3 compares different algorithms (PyPop7 FMAES, LMMAES, and LMCMA against DEAP CMA-ES), confounding implementation efficiency with algorithmic differences. No uncertainty estimates or statistical tests are reported.

The large-scale evaluation uses one fixed dimension and supplies neither dimension-scaling nor memory-scaling results. Its O(d^2) rotation operation can dominate wall-clock time, while hardware, threading, BLAS, Numba warm-up, software versions, and the number of repetitions in Section 3.4 are unspecified. Consequently, the results do not substantiate computational scalability.

Benchmark fairness is unclear: population sizes, initialization, hyperparameter selection, and matched configurations are not documented. DEAP is the only substantive external baseline despite discussion of Nevergrad, PaGMO, EvoSax, and QDax, and a runtime cap combined with a fitness threshold conflates optimizer quality, implementation throughput, and early stopping.

The classification study is insufficiently specified and does not validate ML utility. The five losses are not formally defined; model construction, normalization, train/test splits, and tuning are missing; and only optimization loss is shown, with no held-out accuracy or generalization analysis. Figure 9 duplicates or mislabels "square_loss_lr_qar" in its bottom-right panel, apparently omitting the corresponding tanh-loss task and casting doubt on the claimed 25-task winner counts.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the public code. Links target a mutable main branch rather than an archived release or commit, and the paper provides no environment, hardware specification, raw per-run data, or complete experimental configurations. Table 1 gives unexplained binary self-assessments, contains several N/A entries, and marks FEP "NI," so it does not support the broad correctness claim.

Significance/originality: No new optimizer, theoretical result, or substantive empirical understanding is introduced. The winner-count observations largely partition tasks among whichever method finished first, without significance testing, and do not demonstrate that the library's breadth is necessary. Comparative coverage against existing libraries is asserted rather than quantified.

Presentation is weak: Figures 5-9 compress 20-25 panels and up to 23 curves into single pages without uncertainty bands, making comparisons difficult. The prose contains frequent errors such as "objective-oriented," "Block-Box," and "constrains," along with unsupported promotional descriptions such as "elegant" and "high-quality." The software architecture is described only superficially.

The PDF is not suitable as a blinded ICML main-track submission: it exposes names, emails, affiliations, an identifying repository, and an arXiv watermark, uses a non-ICML template, and has roughly 17 pages of material before the references. These are serious submission-format and anonymity concerns.

Although the future-work list is honest, the manuscript lacks a real threats-to-validity discussion addressing benchmark selection, tuning bias, runtime variability, missing uncertainty, and the limited representativeness of the synthetic and small UCI tasks. Overall, the useful engineering artifact does not compensate for unsupported central performance and scalability claims.

strengths: [Significance] PyPop7 unifies dozens of optimizers from 13 families, with particular attention to large-scale variants; this could be a useful community software artifact. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8pddvemp/call-08ff097289cd4ab4b9a3ad678f45a3a4/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

[Reproducibility] The authors provide GPL-3.0 code, CC-BY documentation, seeded examples, pytest/CI testing, COCO integration, and optimizer-specific repeatability scripts. Table 1 transparently marks unavailable and unsuccessful cases rather than hiding them.

[Evaluation] The experiments span 20 rotated/shifted 2000-dimensional synthetic functions and 25 objectives formed from five losses and five UCI datasets; the classification study uses 15 optimizers and 14 repetitions per task.

[Presentation and ethics] The architecture overview and two code examples make the intended API understandable. Funding and licensing are disclosed, the listed future work identifies several scope gaps, and no substantial direct ethical risk is apparent for this general-purpose optimization library.
weaknesses: [Originality and track fit] The contribution is principally an integration and reimplementation of existing algorithms. The paper introduces no optimizer, theory, benchmark, or convincingly new empirical understanding. A unified API is useful engineering, but the manuscript does not establish the exceptional adoption or capability needed to make this a meaningful ICML main-track research contribution.

[Soundness] Figures 2–4 do not support the broad computational-efficiency claim. They use only one cheap sphere function and one competing library, while several purported implementation comparisons actually pit different algorithms—FMAES, LMMAES, or LMCMA against DEAP CMA-ES—thereby conflating algorithmic complexity with software efficiency. Hardware, library versions, hyperparameters, profiling, memory use, uncertainty, and statistical tests are absent, so the causal attribution to ndarray-based storage is unsupported.

[Soundness] Figures 5–9 provide dense median curves but no dispersion, confidence intervals, aggregate ranks, or significance tests. The number of repetitions for the 20-function study is unspecified. For the classification study, the model, preprocessing, data splits, and held-out predictive metrics are not reported; optimizing training-style losses alone does not demonstrate classification utility or generalization.

[Reproducibility] The hyperlinks target a mutable GitHub main branch rather than an archived release or commit. The manuscript gives no environment lock, dependency versions, hardware specification, or complete experimental configurations. Table 1's self-reported YES labels lack quantitative tolerances or independent validation, and several implementations remain N/A or need improvement.

[Presentation] The related-work comparison is brief and selective, without a systematic feature/coverage comparison against modern alternatives. Several large plot grids have very small labels, and the prose contains recurring grammatical and terminological problems and promotional assertions. The supplied 28-page PDF is author-identified, carries a 2024 arXiv stamp, and is not an anonymous ICML-formatted submission.

[Limitations and ethics] Parallelism, constraint handling, noisy optimization, and automatic algorithm selection are deferred to future work even though they materially limit practical BBO coverage. The paper does not analyze these limitations or report the computational-resource footprint of its many three-hour runs. These issues, together with the unsupported central efficiency claims, require substantially more than a minor revision.

strengths: Significance: PyPop7 is a substantial engineering artifact that places dozens of optimizer variants from many families behind a unified API, with particular attention to high-dimensional optimization.

Reproducibility practices are promising: the authors provide open-source code and documentation, seeded examples, automated pytest/CI checks, and per-optimizer repeatability scripts and results. Table 1 also candidly marks unavailable or unsuccessful reproductions.
The evaluation spans 20 rotated-and-shifted 2000-dimensional functions and 25 loss-function/dataset combinations, while the examples demonstrate both direct use and COCO integration.
The architecture overview and concise code examples make the library approachable. Support for established benchmarking ecosystems could make the artifact useful to practitioners.
No major direct ethical risk is apparent: the experiments use public benchmark datasets and the software and documentation have explicit open licenses.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central computational-efficiency claim is not established fairly. Figures 2–4 frequently compare different algorithms, such as FMAES, LMMAES, or LMCMA against DEAP's CMA-ES, so wall-clock throughput conflates implementation quality with algorithmic complexity and hyperparameters. Results on one sphere function against only DEAP cannot support the claim that PyPop7 implementations are "always better."

The stochastic evidence is inadequate: plots report medians without dispersion, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Only 10 runs are reported for the sphere and 14 for classification, while the run count for Figures 5–8 is unclear. Consequently, the claimed numbers of task wins may be unstable.

Important experimental details are absent, including hardware and threading, software versions, optimizer hyperparameters and tuning protocol, initialization and bounds, construction seeds for rotations and shifts, dataset preprocessing, and commands for regenerating the figures. This particularly undermines three-hour wall-clock comparisons.

The artifact is not frozen: manuscript links point to the mutable GitHub main branch rather than a commit, release, or archive. Table 1 reports binary reproduction success without quantitative tolerances, several methods have no report, and FEP is marked as needing improvement.

Figure 9 appears to duplicate the square_loss_lr_qar panel in its final position, where tanh_loss_lr_qar would be expected; the curves also appear identical. Thus, the advertised 25-task evaluation is at least mislabeled and possibly missing one task, potentially affecting the winner counts.

Originality is mainly engineering aggregation: the paper offers neither a new optimization method nor substantial new scientific understanding. Its related-work analysis is qualitative and limited, with no systematic feature, correctness, memory, or performance comparison against a broader set of modern optimization libraries.

Presentation needs substantial revision: Figures 5–9 are overly dense, numerous grammatical and terminology errors remain, and the conclusion lists constraints, noise, and parallelism only as future work without explaining how their absence limits current applicability. There is also no explicit discussion of compute cost or dataset-related limitations.

Reproducibility intent: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-eznvbpmc/call-81710c3987ef4e52a1fd0fd6fe73b246/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} links public GPL-3.0 code, documentation, examples, pytest/CircleCI testing, explicit seed control, and many per-optimizer repeatability reports.

Experimental breadth: Evaluation includes a 2000-dimensional synthetic setting, 20 rotated-and-shifted functions, and 25 loss/dataset combinations; the classification study runs 15 optimizers 14 times each.
Presentation: The conceptual taxonomy, package organization, and short PyPop7/COCO examples communicate the intended workflow effectively.
Ethics: Licensing and funding are disclosed, the experiments use public benchmarks, and no material privacy, human-subject, or other research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central efficiency claim is not established by a controlled comparison. Figures 3–4 compare different algorithms or variants (e.g., PyPop7 FMAES/LMMAES/LMCMA against DEAP CMA-ES), yet the resulting gap is attributed to implementation choices such as ndarray versus list. Fixed three-hour runs, without matched update rules and hyperparameters, cannot isolate that cause.

Soundness: Results are primarily median convergence curves, with no dispersion, confidence intervals, statistical tests, failure rates, or sensitivity analyses. The number of repetitions is also unspecified for the 20-function study, making the strong statements such as “always better” insufficiently supported.

Benchmark specification is incomplete. Hardware, software versions, optimizer configurations, initialization, shift/rotation generation, and evaluation-counting conventions are missing. For the classification experiments, the predictive model, preprocessing, splits, loss definitions, and held-out metrics are not described; optimizing loss alone does not demonstrate classification quality.

The evaluation offers little independent evidence of competitiveness: beyond DEAP on one sphere function, Figures 5–9 compare PyPop7 algorithms only against one another. There is no systematic comparison with NeverGrad, COCO baselines, SciPy, or other mature implementations, despite positioning the library relative to them.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for the reported claims. Links target a mutable main branch rather than a release tag or commit; no locked environment, container, hardware specification, archived raw results, or end-to-end reproduction command is given. Table 1's self-reported “YES” labels are not quantitative validation, and several implementations are marked N/A or “Need to be Improved.”

Originality is primarily software integration: the paper introduces no new optimizer, theoretical result, benchmark methodology, or substantive empirical insight. Breadth is useful, but the manuscript does not quantify API coverage, correctness, maintenance quality, or advantages over competing libraries sufficiently to establish a main-track research contribution.

Limitations are only indirectly acknowledged through future work. Missing support for constraints, noise, massive parallelism, and automated configuration substantially narrows practical applicability, but their consequences are not analyzed.

Presentation and venue compliance require major revision: dense 20–25-panel plots are difficult to read, several assertions are overstated, and the prose contains recurring errors such as “objective-oriented,” “Block-Box,” and “constrains.” Moreover, the submitted PDF exposes author identities and an arXiv header and uses a roughly 17-page pre-reference, non-ICML format, which is unsuitable for a double-blind ICML main-track submission.

This could be a useful research and teaching resource. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-sk81e39g/call-83b2d24bcdb74478af2fe9deeaf42ef6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Reproducibility and engineering: The GPL-3.0 code, CC-BY documentation, optimizer examples, explicit random-seed interface, automated tests, COCO integration, and per-optimizer repeatability links are valuable practices.

Evaluation breadth: The paper goes beyond a single demonstration, including 20 transformed 2000-dimensional functions, 25 loss-function/dataset combinations based on five public UCI datasets, and runtime comparisons with DEAP.
Presentation: The optimizer taxonomy, conceptual overview, and two executable usage examples communicate the library's intended scope and API reasonably clearly.

Limitations and ethics: The conclusion openly identifies missing support for parallelism, constraints, noise, meta-optimization, and automatic algorithm design. The work uses public datasets and presents no unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The prominent claim that PyPop7 implementations are "always better" than DEAP is not established by Figures 2–4. Only one cheap 2000-dimensional Sphere problem is used, and several comparisons pair different algorithms—for example, PyPop7's specialized large-scale ES variants against DEAP's CMA-ES—so algorithmic differences are confounded with implementation efficiency. Hardware, software versions, threading, equivalent hyperparameters, and profiling results are absent.

Evaluation: Figures 5–9 show median runtime curves without dispersion, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The number of repetitions is not reported for the 20 synthetic functions; the classification study reports 14 runs but no uncertainty. Wall-clock comparisons are hardware-dependent, and no fixed-evaluation-budget analysis or comparison with strong implementations outside PyPop7 is provided.

The classification experiment is underspecified: the five losses are not formally defined, and dataset splits, preprocessing, initialization, hyperparameters, seed schedule, and whether the reported objective corresponds to training or held-out performance are unclear. Consequently, it does not establish optimization robustness or predictive generalization.

Correctness and reproducibility: Table 1's self-reported "YES" entries have no stated numerical tolerance or acceptance protocol; several algorithms are marked N/A and FEP is marked "Need to be Improved." Lightweight unit tests and informal inspection by the authors are insufficient evidence of conformance to dozens of original algorithms. Links target a mutable main branch rather than a pinned release or commit, and the manuscript gives no locked environment or benchmark hardware.

Originality and significance: The contribution is predominantly software integration of existing algorithms, without a new optimization method, theoretical result, benchmark protocol, or clear empirical insight. The related-work section discusses COCO, Nevergrad, DEAP, PyBrain, and PaGMO only qualitatively and provides no systematic feature, coverage, correctness, or performance comparison demonstrating a decisive advance over modern alternatives.

Presentation: Many multi-panel plots are too small to read, and the captions for Figures 6 and 8 visibly run into the footer/page number and are clipped. The prose contains recurrent grammatical errors and promotional assertions stronger than the supplied evidence. As provided, the named authors, emails, arXiv identifier, and non-ICML template also make it unsuitable as a double-blind ICML submission.

Overall, the library may be useful, but the lack of main-track research novelty and the unsupported central claims about correctness and performance are important rather than minor deficiencies. Acceptance would require controlled matched-algorithm benchmarks, uncertainty reporting, complete experimental specifications, a pinned artifact, and substantially stronger positioning and validation.

strengths: Significance: PyPop7 addresses a real engineering need by collecting many black-box optimizers—organized into 13 families, including numerous large-scale variants—behind a common Python API.

Reproducibility effort: the authors provide GPL-licensed code, online documentation, explicit random seeds, pytest/CI testing, per-optimizer examples, repeatability links, and a COCO integration example. These are valuable software-engineering practices.

Presentation: Figure 1 gives a useful overview of the library, while Section 4 makes the basic API readily understandable. The evaluation also spans synthetic functions and classification-derived objectives rather than relying on a single demonstration.

Limitations and ethics: the conclusion candidly identifies unsupported capabilities such as parallelism, constraints, and noisy optimization. The general-purpose optimization software and public benchmark datasets pose no evident major ethical risk, and licensing and funding are disclosed.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central efficiency conclusion is not justified. Figures 2–4 primarily use one unrotated 2000-dimensional Sphere function and often compare different algorithms or variants—for example, PyPop7 large-scale ES variants against DEAP CMA-ES—thereby conflating algorithmic advantages with implementation efficiency. The evidence does not establish the claimed causal explanation that NumPy arrays versus Python lists produce the observed gap or support the broad statement that PyPop7 is “always better.”

Experimental rigor: hardware, software versions, parameter-matching procedures, and timing methodology are not reported. Wall-clock comparisons on objectives with quadratic-cost rotations further confound optimizer overhead with objective-evaluation cost. The paper shows median curves without dispersion, confidence intervals, or statistical tests; it omits the run count for the 20-function study and provides no aggregate ranks or numerical tables from which its winner counts can be verified reliably.

The classification study is too underspecified to support an ML claim. The manuscript does not define the five losses, classifier parameterization, per-dataset dimensionalities, splits, preprocessing, label handling, or optimizer configurations. It evaluates objective loss rather than held-out accuracy or generalization, so Figures 9 cannot demonstrate useful classification performance.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the public repository. Table 1 largely reports author-assigned “YES” outcomes without quantitative tolerances; several optimizers have no report, ESA has no success determination, and FEP is marked “Need to be Improved.” Manual inspection by three authors is not a validation protocol. No immutable commit or release, dependency lockfile, execution environment, raw benchmark records, or complete commands/configurations are specified in the paper.

Originality is limited to software integration and reimplementation: no new optimizer, analysis, or substantive empirical insight is introduced. The related-work discussion offers only qualitative assertions about a few libraries and lacks a systematic coverage, correctness, usability, memory, or speed comparison with contemporary alternatives. Consequently, the main-track research contribution and incremental value over existing ecosystems are not convincingly established.

Significance is asserted more than demonstrated. Reported applications are anecdotal, while adoption, maintenance quality, API stability, test coverage, and independent correctness are not measured. Major practical regimes—constraints, noise, and parallel or accelerated execution—are deferred to future work, substantially narrowing the library’s present reach.

Presentation is below conference standard. Figures 5–9 compress 20–25 panels and up to 23 legend entries into single pages, making labels and individual curves difficult to read; captions omit essential setup details. Numerous grammatical and typographical problems further reduce precision.

The manuscript has no dedicated limitations or ethics discussion and does not explicitly bound its conclusions around benchmark selection, hardware dependence, missing validation, or training-only classification losses. Additionally, the submitted PDF contains author names, affiliations, emails, acknowledgments, direct repository links, and an arXiv identifier, so it is not anonymized for an ICML main-track review. Overall, the library has discernible utility, but the technical and evidential deficiencies require substantial revision before its claims can be relied upon.

Figures 2-4 claim PyPop7 is always better than DEAP and attribute the difference to NumPy arrays versus Python lists, but Figure 3 compares FMAES, LMMAES, and LMCMA against a different algorithm, DEAP's full CMA-ES. Algorithmic and asymptotic differences therefore confound implementation efficiency. There is no profiling or ablation establishing the asserted cause.

The DEAP experiment uses only ten runs on one unrotated Sphere problem at dimension 2000. Hardware, dependency versions, process configuration, hyperparameters, implementation equivalence, and uncertainty are unreported. The related-work comparison is narrow and lacks a systematic feature or performance comparison with contemporary alternatives. This limits the contribution for the ICML main research track, even if the library could be valuable in a software venue.

Presentation is polished at the structural level but weak in execution. Figures 5-9 contain 20-25 tiny panels with many overlapping curves and no uncertainty; Figure 7's axis text visibly collides with its caption. Frequent grammatical errors and imprecise terminology further impede interpretation.

There is no substantive limitations discussion or ethics statement. The conclusion merely lists missing capabilities such as massive parallelism, constraint handling, and noisy optimization as future work, without explaining how these omissions delimit present claims. No major ethical concern is evident, but dataset provenance/licensing and potential misuse are not discussed.

strengths: Significance: PyPop7 is a potentially useful engineering resource, collecting dozens of black-box optimizers across 13 stated families behind a unified API, with particular attention to large-scale variants. The COCO integration example and two compact usage examples make the practical intent concrete. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-1msapgov/call-45900fe94bcb40208263b8fd2cc1933d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Originality: The individual optimization methods are established, but assembling many specialized large-scale variants in a consistent pure-Python interface is a nontrivial and relatively distinctive software contribution.

Reproducibility: The public GPL-3.0 code, CC-BY documentation, explicit random-seed option, pytest/CI testing, per-optimizer examples, and linked repeatability scripts are valuable foundations for reusable research software.

Soundness—positive evidence: The authors undertake a sizable evaluation effort, including repeated runs, 2000-dimensional synthetic problems, 20 rotated-and-shifted functions, and 25 classification objectives constructed from five UCI datasets and five losses.
Presentation: The high-level architecture, optimizer taxonomy, and API examples communicate the library's intended structure and basic use reasonably clearly.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central efficiency comparison does not isolate implementation quality. Figures 3–4 frequently compare different algorithms or variants—for example, PyPop7 FMAES/LMMAES against DEAP CMA-ES—on only the sphere function under a fixed runtime. Consequently, differences in evaluations completed and solution quality conflate algorithm behavior, hyperparameters, and implementation speed. Counting more evaluations within three hours measures throughput, not optimization efficiency by itself, so the claim that PyPop7 implementations are “always better” is unsupported.

Soundness: Results are reported mainly as median curves without dispersion, confidence intervals, statistical tests, failure rates, or numerical result tables. Initializations, domains, transformations, population sizes, tuning procedures, and fairness controls are largely absent. The finite-benchmark observation that different methods win different tasks also does not establish the claimed connection to the No Free Lunch theorem.

Soundness: The classification study is insufficiently specified and does not establish ML utility. The manuscript omits precise model parameterizations, loss definitions, train/validation/test splits, preprocessing details, and predictive metrics. Comparing training-objective convergence alone cannot support conclusions about classification accuracy or generalization.

Reproducibility: All implementation and result links target mutable GitHub “main” or documentation “latest” pages rather than an archived release or commit. The manuscript gives no hardware, operating system, package versions, complete configurations, seeds for each run, or executable workflow for the reported three-hour experiments. Table 1's self-reported YES labels provide no tolerances or quantitative checks; several entries are N/A or “need to be improved,” while manual inspection by the authors is not adequate correctness validation.

Significance/originality: This is principally a software aggregation paper and offers no new optimization algorithm, theory, benchmark methodology, or well-supported empirical finding. Comparisons are mostly internal or against the much older DEAP library, with limited treatment of contemporary optimizer libraries and external state-of-the-art solvers. The useful engineering contribution therefore does not reach the ICML main research-track bar in its present evidential form.

Presentation: Figures 5–9 place up to 23 curves across dense grids with very small labels, making substantive comparison difficult; aggregate ranks or statistical summaries are absent. Numerous grammatical problems, imprecise terminology such as “objective-oriented programming,” and repeated promotional or absolute language further reduce clarity. The submitted PDF also exposes author identities, emails, and an arXiv identifier rather than presenting an anonymized ICML submission.

Limitations and ethics: The future-work list acknowledges missing support for parallelism, constraints, and noise, but the paper provides no substantive limitations discussion qualifying its scalability or benchmark claims. No acute ethical hazard is apparent and funding is disclosed, yet there is no ethics/broader-impact discussion, including for the human-derived Parkinson's dataset, dataset licensing and demographic bias, or potentially harmful uses such as black-box adversarial attacks. These ethical omissions are secondary to the technical concerns.

Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess soundness, presentation, significance, and originality separately before forming the overall recommendation. Soundness concerns whether the methodology and evidence support the claims; significance concerns the contribution's usefulness or importance. Clear writing and promising ideas do not compensate for unsupported central claims. A modest or specialized contribution can still be useful, and originality may arise through new understanding rather than an entirely new method.

Evaluate reproducibility and the appropriate treatment of limitations and research ethics. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses using evidence from the manuscript. Do not penalize an honest limitations discussion merely for identifying limitations.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
The submission has fundamental deficiencies or lacks a discernible contribution that could justify acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important technical, evidential, reproducibility, presentation, or ethical weaknesses prevent acceptance.

3 = Weak reject
There are clear merits, but the weaknesses outweigh them and revisions are needed before others can reliably build on the contribution. Please use sparingly.

4 = Weak accept
The work is technically solid and advances an area in a useful way, while limitations reduce its reach or strength. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper combines technical solidity with a meaningful contribution, convincing evaluation, and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work makes an exceptional, well-supported contribution with outstanding technical quality and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

strengths: [Significance] The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2026--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8czzekby/call-7629b577faea4ff58cb69576b24d4ba0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a potentially useful engineering resource: a unified API spanning 13 optimizer families and roughly 76 implementations, with particular coverage of large-scale variants.

[Reproducibility] The GPL-3.0 repository, CC-BY documentation, optimizer-specific scripts/results, explicit seed interface, pytest/CI workflow, and COCO integration are commendable efforts toward reusable research software.
[Presentation] The architecture overview and two concrete code examples make the intended workflow accessible, and the motivation for collecting population-based black-box optimizers is clear.

[Evaluation scope] The experiments are ambitious in breadth, covering a 2000-dimensional timing benchmark, 20 transformed synthetic functions, and 25 loss/dataset combinations; the classification study reports 14 independent runs per optimizer-task pair.

[Ethics] The contribution is general-purpose infrastructure evaluated mainly on synthetic or public UCI data, so no immediate material ethical concern is apparent; funding and software licensing are disclosed.
weaknesses: [Soundness] Figures 2-4 do not substantiate the central efficiency claim. They use only one 2000-dimensional sphere function, report medians from ten runs without uncertainty or tests, omit hardware, dependency versions, hyperparameters, population sizes, and JIT/warm-up treatment, and sometimes compare different algorithms—e.g., PyPop7 FMAES/LMMAES/LMCMA against DEAP CMA-ES. Consequently, neither the claim that PyPop7 is “always better” nor the causal attribution to ndarray-based storage is established; profiling or controlled ablations are absent.

[Soundness] Figures 5-8 provide only dense median curves. The number of repetitions is not stated, dispersion and statistical comparisons are absent, transformation instances and initialization settings are unspecified, and no numerical tables or aggregate ranks are given. A three-hour wall-clock budget on quadratically expensive rotated objectives also conflates optimizer quality with implementation and objective-evaluation throughput. Comparisons only among PyPop7 methods cannot validate correctness or competitiveness against canonical external implementations.

[Soundness] The classification benchmark is insufficiently defined: the classifier/model, exact five loss functions, regularization, preprocessing, train/validation/test splits, dimensions, and evaluation metric are not specified. Figure 9 reports optimization fitness rather than predictive generalization and again omits uncertainty. The explanation that COCMA exploits sparsity is speculative, and invoking No-Free-Lunch to explain observed rank diversity is not a valid inference from that theorem.

[Reproducibility] Table 1 is useful but not compelling verification of implementation correctness. Seven optimizers have no repeatability code/results, ESA has an N/A success status, and FEP is marked “Need to be Improved”; the remaining YES labels lack reported tolerances or independent reference checks. Author inspection and lightweight tests are not substitutes for validated numerical equivalence or documented test coverage.

[Reproducibility] Repository links target a mutable main branch rather than an archived release or commit. The paper supplies no complete environment lockfile, package versions, hardware specification, seed schedule, raw benchmark tables, or self-contained experiment configuration, so the reported results cannot be reliably reconstructed from the manuscript.

[Originality and significance] The research contribution is predominantly integration and reimplementation; no new optimization method, analysis, or empirically derived insight is introduced. The related-work comparison is narrow and dated, discussing COCO, NeverGrad, DEAP, PyBrain, and PaGMO without a systematic feature/performance comparison against other contemporary optimization ecosystems. Thus the claimed distinctiveness and 2026 main-track significance are not convincingly established.

[Presentation] The plots containing 9-23 curves across 20-25 tiny panels are difficult to read and lack supporting result tables. The text also contains recurring errors such as “objective-oriented,” “Block-Box,” and “constrains,” while giving little architectural detail beyond inheritance and a unified constructor. The author-identifying arXiv/JMLR-style, 18-page main text is also not presented as an anonymous ICML main-track submission.

[Limitations and ethics] The paper has no substantive limitations discussion. The conclusion lists parallelism, constraints, noise, and meta-learning as future work but does not delimit current API coverage, scalability, correctness risk, or benchmark validity. Given the extensive three-hour runs and the stated applicability to black-box attacks, compute footprint and dual-use considerations would also merit brief treatment, although these are secondary to the evidential deficiencies.
